title: Questions and Answers on Chán-Inquiry Buddha-Recitation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Answer: The achievement of Buddha-recitation comes when reciting is unmingled with wandering thoughts — when the thought of recitation continues unbroken into a single, seamless piece. Master Yinguang said: "If Buddha-recitation cannot yet be made pure and single, you must restrain the mind and not let it stray outward; in time it will naturally become pure and single. 'Becoming one seamless piece' means being pure and single, without admixture." (from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings, Letter Four in Reply to Layman Ma Qixi)

inline.s: Question: What does it mean for the practice of Buddha-recitation to become one seamless piece?

Answer: The achievement of Buddha-recitation is attained when, in reciting the Buddha's name, no wandering thoughts are mixed in — when the thought of recitation continues unbroken into a single, seamless piece. Master Yinguang said:

"If Buddha-recitation cannot yet be made pure and single, you must restrain the mind and not let it stray outward; in time it will naturally become pure and single. 'Becoming one seamless piece' means being pure and single, without admixture."
(from Master Yinguang's Collected Writings
Letter Four in Reply to Layman Ma Qixi.) Master Hanshan said:
"You must take this one sound of the Buddha's name
(the Buddha's name)
and bite down on it,
determined to overcome the deluded thoughts

. In every place, keep it present in every thought, and do not let deluded thoughts cover and obstruct it. If you apply such bitter, earnest effort, in time it will ripen and mature, and you will naturally attain a response; without seeking the seamless piece, it will become seamless of itself."
(from the Dream Wanderings Collection
"Instructions to the Layman Jingxin.")
Question: When I practice Chán-inquiry Buddha-recitation, my wandering thoughts have grown far fewer, but when drowsiness comes over me, I am at a loss. How should I counteract drowsiness?

Answer: When drowsiness comes over you, you may pause the inquiry to counteract it. The method is this: rouse your spirits, and from time to time raise your head and gaze upward, while doing deep abdominal breathing — inhale deeply through the nose (the abdomen bulges outward), hold the breath
second, then exhale slowly (the abdomen sinks inward), hold the breath
second, and keep each full inhalation and exhalation to about

seconds. At the same time, recite the Buddha's name (on the in-breath recite "A-mi," on the out-breath "tuo-fo"), and be clearly aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen. In this way the drowsiness will gradually recede. Once it has passed, return to the Chán-inquiry Buddha-recitation. You may also adopt the method taught by the ancients in Whip for Advancing Through the Chán Gate (compiled by Master Lianchi):
Brethren, if you have long been dozing on the meditation cushion
(long fallen into drowsiness)

, you must get down and walk a round, rinse your mouth and wash your eyes with cold water, and then return to the cushion. Straighten your spine, stand firm as a cliff ten thousand fathoms high, and single-mindedly raise the huatou."
Of late, few are those who sincerely devote themselves to Chán. No sooner does one raise a huatou than one is entangled by the two demons of dullness
(drowsiness)
and scattering
(distraction)
, not knowing that dullness and scattering are precisely countered by the doubt-sensation
(not knowing that the doubt-sensation is exactly the sharp weapon for countering dullness and scattering)
. When faith is deep, the doubt-sensation is bound to be deep; and when the doubt-sensation is deep, dullness and scattering vanish of themselves."
One day in the corridor I saw Xiu
(the senior seat Xiu)
, and only then could I draw near.
I therefore asked: 'At present, drowsiness and scattering cannot be driven away
(I cannot dispel my drowsiness and distraction — what shall I do?)

.' Xiu said: 'That is because you yourself are not fierce enough! You must sit high on the cushion, straighten your spine, and make your whole body into one single huatou — then where will drowsiness and scattering be found
(where would there still be any drowsiness or distraction)
?' I did my practice according to Xiu's words
(so I practiced according to the senior seat Xiu's words)
, and unaware, both body and mind were forgotten. Clear and pure for three days and nights, my two eyes never closed."
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, be utterly destitute
(entirely free of attachments)
, and look into this: before my father and mother were born, which
(which one)
was my original face? Whether or not it proves effective, whether or not there is dullness and scattering, just keep raising it."

If there is dullness and scattering, do not arouse a thought to drive them away; quickly raise the huatou, shake body and mind awake, and summon your energy with full vigor. If that still does not work, get down and do walking meditation; when you sense the dullness and scattering have passed, return to the cushion. Suddenly it will be raised without being raised, and doubted without being doubted. Walking, you know not that you walk; sitting, you know not that you sit. There is only the feeling of inquiry, aloof and solitary, distinct and clear. This is called the place where afflictions are cut off, and also the place where the self is lost."
Question: If the huatou is the word "Wu" (Nothing), how should one investigate it?
Answer: If you are investigating the word "Wu," then probe inward: who is it that raises this word "Wu"?
Master Hanshan said:

"Single-mindedly raise one gong'an huatou, such as 'Zhaozhou — does a dog have the Buddha-nature or not? — Zhaozhou said, Wu,' or 'The ten thousand dharmas return to the One; where does the One return?' or investigate 'Who is it that recites the Buddha's name?' Take up any one of these and lay it across your chest like the vajra king's sword, cutting off all thoughts and deluded fancies at once, as one cuts through tangled silk. Within, allow nothing to come out; without, allow nothing to go in; seize the vital pass, block the throat, and permit no breath to pass. Apply your strength thus,
and with one glance look straight at: what, after all, is this thing that raises the huatou?
(from the Dream Wanderings Collection, "Instructions to the Mountain Master Songpu'en")

Question: I raise the Buddha's name and then probe inward: who is it that recites the Buddha's name? In this way my wandering thoughts grow fewer and fewer, and my practice gradually gains strength. My question is this: after investigating like this for a long time, my head grows dizzy; and sometimes I find the practice hard to do, yet if I grit my teeth and press on, I also grow dizzy. What should I do?

Answer: This shows that your power of awareness is not yet strong enough. You may resolve your problem this way: whenever you meet trouble — dizziness, for example — go back to the preparatory practices. When these go smoothly, return to the inquiry. Persisting in this back-and-forth, your inquiry will grow more and more effective, and you will no longer grow dizzy. At the same time, remember this lesson of experience in doing practice: you must not hurry, and you must not stop. Remind yourself of this at all times.

Question: My Chán-inquiry Buddha-recitation was going very well, but somehow I have suffered a great setback! No matter how I investigate, it will not go well; agitation, weariness, and drowsiness follow one after another, and even deluded thoughts hover about and will not leave. What should I do?

Answer: This is not a great setback, but rather the arrival of practice at its most critical juncture: the practice has gained such strength that the karmic seeds accumulated over countless kalpas and stored within the ālaya-vijñāna have been pressed hard and forced to burst out. You must meet this calmly and hold your ground. The way to deal with it is summed up in a single word: endure. Endure with the passion and perseverance kindled by true faith and earnest vows — endure through it and victory is yours! Therefore, at such a time you must rouse your spirits and never set down the Buddha's name. "You fight your fight, I'll fight mine" — so long as I simply look after my own recitation, the boat will never capsize! While enduring does mean gritting your teeth, this refers chiefly to an unshakable faith and a determination that will not bow before difficulty. But in the actual doing of it, there is no harm in a touch of humor, even with a smile on your face, as if to say: let's see what you can do to me! Remember, this is the darkness before dawn. Endure through this pass, and it is a great victory.
[When the karmic seeds of countless kalpas are pressed hard] In his Letter in Reply to Layman Mao Jingquan, Mr. Jiang Weinong gives this account of his own experience:
I recall that five years ago, I
(Mr. Jiang Weinong refers to himself)
was in Beijing, and one day, while I was reciting the Buddha's name
(one day, at the very time of reciting the Buddha's name)
, a great evil thought suddenly arose, and I was so terrified that sweat poured from me as though I had been washed
(drenched in sweat)
, so that for several days I dared not do my daily practice. Then I reflected
(afterward I reflected)
that in my whole life I had never had such a thought, so whence did this thought arise? Perhaps
it was the karmic seeds of many past lives
(perhaps it was the karmic seeds stored in the ālaya-vijñāna over many lifetimes)
? I tried to console myself a little
(I slightly comforted myself)
. Yet in the end I could not resolve the doubt
(yet what exactly it was, I could not be certain)
. Later I asked the Venerable Di
xian, the Dharma master
(later I consulted Dharma Master Dixian)
, and Master Di said: 'These are the seeds of many past lives
(these are the karmic seeds of many past lives)
, now smoked and pressed out by the power of the Buddha
through this intensified effort, the roots can be pulled out
(you can thereby uproot these karmic seeds)
Master Hanshan, in his
Letter in Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan, gives this instruction as well:

When your practice reaches the point of genuine strength and outer objects no longer enter, only the inner afflictions remain, suddenly rising on all sides for no reason. Either lustful thoughts flare up, or the mind grows vexed and oppressed, or all manner of hindrances arise, until the mind is weary and the strength spent, and nothing can be done. These are the seeds of habit accumulated over countless kalpas, stored within the ālaya-vijñāna
(also called karmic seeds)

, now pressed hard by your practice and brought forth. This is the most critical juncture; you must have a clear measure of it in your own mind, and must first see through them, pass beyond them, and by no means let them envelop you, toy with you, or be taken as real matters. Only rouse your spirits, strive with brave vigor, and raise your own root huatou. If the lustful thoughts and afflictions still hover and will not leave, then at the very point where these thoughts arise, press your pursuit straight onward: here in me, this matter has never existed at all — ask whence it comes, and what after all it is; resolve to see its final landing-place. Pressing down like this, you will make even gods and ghosts weep, and the traces will vanish and the tracks disappear. You must be sure to exterminate them utterly, not leaving a single thread.
Applying your strength thus, you will naturally come to see good news.
(For the original text, see
The Essentials of Chán and Pure Land
the section "The Essentials of Practice and Awakening.")

Furthermore, when agitation (or weariness, or drowsiness) arises, observe carefully just what kind of sensation it is. As you observe it in this way, the agitation (or weariness, or drowsiness) will gradually become less intense and less disturbing, and the mind will slowly settle into peace.
